title: Choose grain before columns
prompt: A source export repeats order header totals on every line. Analysts need quantity and net revenue by product and customer. You must retain line-level detail and avoid double counting. Which fact design is appropriate?

options.text: One row per order line, with line measures and dimension keys; keep header totals at their own grain.
options.why: The line grain supports product analysis without summing duplicated order-level totals.

options.text: One row per order line, storing and summing the full order total on each row.
options.why: Repeating the header total causes each order to contribute once per line.

options.text: One row per customer, with the latest product and cumulative order quantity.
options.why: This loses the requested product and order-line detail and mixes entities with events.

options.text: One row per order, assigning its total to the first product on that order.
options.why: This cannot correctly allocate the total across the order's different products.

explanation: Choose a consistent event grain before choosing measures. A duplicated header amount is not an additive line measure.

title: Flatten a hierarchy deliberately
prompt: Products belong to subcategories and categories. Report authors need one Category > Subcategory > Product hierarchy and direct filtering of a large sales fact. There is no separate need to manage category entities in the semantic model. Which design best fits?

options.text: Retain three dimension tables and build one model hierarchy across all three tables.
options.why: A model hierarchy cannot span columns from separate tables in this manner.

options.text: Copy every product description and hierarchy label into every fact row.
options.why: This increases fact width and mixes descriptive attributes with event storage.

options.text: Combine the hierarchy attributes in one product dimension with one product key relationship to sales.
options.why: A single dimension allows the requested hierarchy and a shorter filter path.

options.text: Use CategoryId alone as the product dimension key and keep all product rows.
options.why: Products in one category share the key, so it cannot uniquely identify product rows.

explanation: Flattening a snowflake dimension can improve model usability. It does not mean copying every descriptive column into the fact.

title: Separate topology from history
prompt: A consultant says you must convert a star schema to a snowflake before customer-region history can be preserved. Which response is correct?

options.text: Split Region into a lookup table and overwrite Customer.RegionId on every move, retaining sales' existing CustomerSK.
options.why: Normalization alone still restates older sales when the referenced customer's RegionId is overwritten.

options.text: Keep a star if it fits reporting, and version the customer dimension independently using SCD2.
options.why: Normalization and change-history policy are distinct design decisions.

options.text: Keep a star, replace CustomerSK on all past sales with the latest version key, and retain old dimension rows.
options.why: Retaining unreferenced rows does not preserve the original assignment after every past fact is remapped.

options.text: Keep one customer row and record its last two regions in columns for unlimited historical moves.
options.why: A limited previous-region column cannot preserve an unrestricted assignment history.

explanation: Star versus snowflake describes table structure. SCD describes what the load does when selected attributes change.

title: Identify a measure by meaning
prompt: An order-line export has OrderId = 9001, CustomerId = 44, Quantity = 3, and NetAmount = 120. Select TWO columns that can be summed meaningfully across compatible lines in one currency.

options.text: OrderId
options.why: An identifier labels an event; adding identifiers does not measure business activity.

options.text: Quantity
options.why: Units are additive across the compatible order-line grain specified here.

options.text: CustomerId
options.why: Numeric storage does not turn a customer identifier into an additive measure.

options.text: NetAmount
options.why: Amounts are additive under the question's compatible currency and line-grain assumptions.

explanation: Classify columns by analytical meaning, not by whether their data type is numeric.

title: Repair the one-side key
prompt: DimCustomer has CustomerId C1 twice for two historical regions, with unique CustomerSK values 10 and 11. FactSales currently stores only CustomerId and SaleTime. Historical reporting is required. Select TWO necessary design steps.

options.text: Resolve the version by CustomerId and SaleTime during preparation and store its CustomerSK on each fact.
options.why: Each sale must identify the dimension version appropriate to its event time.

options.text: Declare CustomerId unique while retaining both versions and use it as the one-side key.
options.why: The repeated business identifier is not unique at dimension-version grain.

options.text: Relate DimCustomer[CustomerSK] one-to-many to FactSales[CustomerSK].
options.why: The unique version key supplies the intended one-side relationship.

options.text: Drop all expired dimension rows so CustomerId becomes unique.
options.why: Deleting those rows loses the historical context required by the problem.

explanation: A business identity names the entity; a surrogate identifies its particular stored version. Prepare fact keys before creating the model relationship.

title: Interpret unenforced declarations
prompt: An existing Fabric Warehouse dimension contains duplicate CustomerSK values. You add PRIMARY KEY NONCLUSTERED (CustomerSK) NOT ENFORCED. What must the team do before relying on a one-to-many semantic relationship?

options.text: Refresh the model; the declaration repairs duplicate keys automatically.
options.why: An unenforced declaration does not deduplicate the stored rows.

options.text: Add a NOT ENFORCED foreign key; it rejects every orphan and duplicate.
options.why: These declarations do not enforce the needed data-integrity rules.

options.text: Replace CustomerSK with the repeated natural CustomerId.
options.why: A repeated natural key cannot identify each historical version uniquely.

options.text: Detect and repair duplicates and orphan mappings in the load, then verify the one-side key is unique.
options.why: Integrity must be validated by the preparation process rather than assumed from metadata.

explanation: Fabric Warehouse PK, UNIQUE, and FK support is NOT ENFORCED. Declare truthful metadata only after validating the data.

title: Apply a governed immutable value
prompt: A fiscal calendar stores the approved original fiscal-period assignment. Policy forbids changing that field after approval; exceptional errors require a separately audited correction process. A normal source feed proposes a different period. Which load behavior follows the policy?

options.text: Treat the governed field as SCD0 in the normal load and route the discrepancy for review.
options.why: Normal processing preserves the approved value while exposing an exception explicitly.

options.text: Overwrite the approved field but retain the incoming file as an audit artifact.
options.why: Retaining evidence does not satisfy the rule that the normal load must preserve the approved assignment.

options.text: Insert a new period version automatically and make subsequent facts use it.
options.why: Versioning is plausible, but adopting the unapproved replacement violates this question's fixed-assignment policy.

options.text: Store the approved period as PreviousPeriod and make the incoming value current.
options.why: Keeping the prior value still changes which assignment is current without the required approval.

explanation: SCD0 is a chosen load policy. It does not prove that every source value is correct or ban an explicitly governed correction process.

title: Select attribute-level behavior
prompt: A customer dimension must show corrected spelling everywhere, but must retain the sales territory effective when each sale occurred. Which policy satisfies both requirements?

options.text: SCD2 for spelling; SCD1 for territory.
options.why: This retains unwanted spelling history while restating territory and losing required history.

options.text: SCD3 for both fields, retaining only the previous values.
options.why: One prior territory cannot provide an unrestricted history of assignments.

options.text: SCD1 for spelling corrections; SCD2 for territory changes.
options.why: Correction and historical assignment are separate attribute-level requirements.

options.text: SCD0 for both fields after the customer first appears.
options.why: Neither subsequent corrections nor actual territory changes would be reflected.

explanation: Different columns of the same dimension can have different history policies. Decide from the required reporting semantics.

title: Explain a changed historical grouping
prompt: One customer has sales 100 in West. Its sole dimension row uses SCD1, and its region is overwritten with East. Fact amounts and keys are unchanged. After refresh, which result follows when sales are grouped through that dimension?

options.text: West = 100 and East = 100 because the overwrite adds a sale.
options.why: Changing a dimension attribute does not add another fact event.

options.text: East = 100 and West has no sales from this customer; total remains 100.
options.why: The same fact now groups under the latest region, with unchanged amount.

options.text: West = 100 because fact foreign keys automatically store old labels.
options.why: A key does not snapshot the previous descriptive attribute on its own.

options.text: Total becomes zero because a type 1 update invalidates every foreign key.
options.why: Updating a non-key attribute preserves the key and existing fact linkage.

explanation: Type 1 can restate historical groupings even though fact measures remain intact. That is correct only when current-state grouping is intended.

title: A refresh cannot invent lost versions
prompt: A source exposes only today's customer row. The imported dimension is fully replaced nightly; no prior source snapshots or change log exist. The business now asks for last year's region assignments. What is the correct assessment?

options.text: Begin nightly SCD2 capture now and use today's row as the assignment for every date last year.
options.why: Future capture is useful, but backdating today's value does not establish last year's actual assignments.

options.text: Retain historical fact partitions and join them to the fully refreshed current dimension.
options.why: Those facts retain sales, while the refreshed dimension still lacks earlier assignment values.

options.text: Assign new surrogate keys on every full refresh and infer regions from key ordering.
options.why: Generated key order is not evidence of missing historical values or effective dates.

options.text: Recover historical evidence if available elsewhere, and establish version capture for future changes.
options.why: Historical reporting requires source history or history that the load retained.

explanation: SCD2 preserves captured changes. Merely adding its column names cannot reconstruct history that has been discarded.

title: Resolve the shared boundary
prompt: A customer has SK 5 valid [January 1, April 1) and SK 6 valid [April 1, infinity). A sale occurs exactly April 1 at 00:00 UTC. Which version should its fact reference?

options.text: SK 6 only.
options.why: The old interval excludes its end; the new interval includes its start.

options.text: SK 5 only.
options.why: The sale is not earlier than the old version's exclusive end.

options.text: Both SK 5 and SK 6.
options.why: A valid half-open chain has exactly one match at the shared boundary.

options.text: Neither version.
options.why: The new interval includes that precise instant, so there is no gap.

explanation: The lab adopts half-open intervals: EventTime >= ValidFrom AND EventTime < ValidTo. One shared boundary then belongs to the new version.

title: Select the temporal join
prompt: ValidTo is a non-null future sentinel for current rows. Every version interval is half-open. Which predicate resolves the dimension version for a fact's event timestamp?

options.text: f.CustomerId = d.CustomerId AND d.IsCurrent = 1
options.why: This selects today's assignment even when the fact occurred in an older interval.

options.text: f.CustomerId = d.CustomerId AND f.EventTime BETWEEN d.ValidFrom AND d.ValidTo
options.why: BETWEEN includes both boundaries, potentially matching two adjacent versions.

options.text: f.CustomerId = d.CustomerId AND f.EventTime >= d.ValidFrom AND f.EventTime < d.ValidTo
options.why: The identifier and both interval bounds identify the event-time version.

options.text: f.CustomerId = d.CustomerId AND f.EventTime >= d.ValidFrom
options.why: Omitting the end bound lets later events match expired versions too.

explanation: Choose the temporal predicate at preparation time; the semantic model then relates facts to a unique version key.
code:
-- Contract: ValidTo is non-null; intervals are [ValidFrom, ValidTo).
SELECT d.CustomerSK FROM FactStage f JOIN DimCustomer d ON /* predicate */;

title: Support a null current end
prompt: Current versions use ValidTo = NULL instead of a sentinel. Which end-date condition correctly completes an otherwise valid half-open temporal join?

options.text: f.EventTime <= d.ValidTo OR d.IsCurrent = 1
options.why: The inclusive end can overlap, and a flag does not replace coherent interval bounds.

options.text: f.EventTime < d.ValidTo OR d.ValidTo IS NULL
options.why: With the start condition already applied, this accepts an open end or an unexpired bounded interval.

options.text: f.EventTime < d.ValidTo OR d.ValidTo = NULL
options.why: Equality to NULL evaluates as unknown and fails to recognize an open end.

options.text: d.ValidTo IS NOT NULL
options.why: This excludes every current version and does not compare the event to the end.

explanation: For null-ended intervals, use EventTime >= ValidFrom AND (EventTime < ValidTo OR ValidTo IS NULL). Keep the parentheses when combined with other predicates.
code:
WHERE f.CustomerId = d.CustomerId
  AND f.EventTime >= d.ValidFrom
  AND ( /* end-date condition */ )

title: Handle a late fact
prompt: A sale dated February arrives in August. The dimension's February and August versions are retained with complete valid intervals. Historical assignment is required. What should the loader do?

options.text: Use the August current version because August is the load date.
options.why: Arrival time is not the event time required for historical assignment.

options.text: Insert another dimension version at August for this old sale.
options.why: An old event does not itself establish a new customer attribute change.

options.text: Use the smallest surrogate key without checking its validity.
options.why: Key order does not establish whether a version covers February.

options.text: Look up the business identifier against the February event timestamp and store that version key.
options.why: The retained interval history allows the fact to resolve its original context.

explanation: Late arrival and late effective change are different problems. This question provides complete history, so event-time lookup is sufficient.

title: Reject an ambiguous match
prompt: Customer C4 has two version intervals that both contain June 10. A June 10 fact therefore matches two rows. Which action best preserves historical correctness?

options.text: Quarantine the ambiguous mapping and repair the overlapping chain before publishing that fact.
options.why: Without a unique valid match, silently choosing a version invents an unsupported assignment.

options.text: Pick MAX(CustomerSK), because a higher key proves a later effective assignment.
options.why: A surrogate's numerical value is not an authoritative effective-time policy.

options.text: Duplicate the fact once per version so both histories are represented.
options.why: This multiplies fact measures and does not repair the invalid version chain.

options.text: Use DISTINCT on amount after joining, regardless of the other columns.
options.why: It can collapse real equal-valued sales and leaves the assignment ambiguous.

explanation: Temporal preparation requires exactly one intended version match. Neither TOP 1 nor DISTINCT is a substitute for repairing conflicting history.

title: Count a faulty natural-key join
prompt: A fact has one sale amount 80 for Customer C1. Its dimension has three C1 versions with unique surrogate keys. SQL joins only on CustomerId, with no interval or current filter, and sums the joined amount. What result does that query produce?

options.text: 80, because unique surrogate keys stop repeated natural-key matches.
options.why: The query does not join on those surrogate keys, so each C1 row matches.

options.text: 160, because only expired versions are included automatically.
options.why: No predicate restricts the join to expired rows or a particular count.

options.text: 240, because the single sale matches three dimension rows.
options.why: The join creates three rows, each containing the amount 80.

options.text: 0, because duplicate natural identifiers prevent SQL joins.
options.why: SQL permits multiple matches and returns them unless restricted by the query.

explanation: Reason about join cardinality before aggregation. Unique version keys do not protect a query that joins on a different repeated column.

title: Choose the complete SCD2 change
prompt: One current customer version has Region = West. A validated effective change sets Region = East at T. Which write set preserves its history under the supplied [start,end) convention?

options.text: Overwrite Region in the current row and keep its surrogate key.
options.why: That is a type 1 overwrite and removes the old assignment.

options.text: Expire the old row at T and insert a new row with a new surrogate, ValidFrom = T, and current status.
options.why: Both steps preserve the old version and establish the new one at the same boundary.

options.text: Insert a new current row but leave the old row current and unbounded.
options.why: This creates competing current versions and overlapping validity.

options.text: Expire the old row and reuse its surrogate key on a new row with different attributes.
options.why: Reusing a version identity can make existing facts ambiguous or restated.

explanation: A historical change is an expiration plus a replacement version. Both must satisfy the key and interval invariants.

title: Order an atomic version change
prompt: Changed rows and new unique surrogate keys have already been materialized; no concurrent writer is allowed. This loader's insertion step requires the old-version keys returned by a successful expiration step and validates its affected-row count before insertion. Put these four actions in order to publish one coherent SCD2 change.

options.text: Expire the old current version using the staged effective timestamp.
options.why: Expiration belongs inside the same atomic operation as its replacement.

options.text: Commit the transaction after the replacement and load control writes succeed.
options.why: Commit makes the complete new chain and its control record visible together.

options.text: Begin a Warehouse transaction.
options.why: The transaction must begin before the version-modifying statements.

options.text: Insert the staged replacement version and its applied-change control record.
options.why: The staged row survives expiration and supplies the replacement and replay identity.

explanation: The stated insertion dependency requires expiration first; the transaction begins before either write and commits after both. Without that dependency, insert-before-expire can also be atomic, so this is a loader-specific order rather than a universal SQL rule.

title: Repair null-sensitive detection
prompt: A loader tracks Region changes with t.Region <> s.Region. Target Region is NULL; source Region is 'East'. What happens, and what is the appropriate repair?

options.text: It detects the change because NULL is different from every non-null string.
options.why: That is a business interpretation of missingness; ordinary SQL inequality involving NULL yields unknown.

options.text: It misses the change; add t.Region IS NOT NULL AND s.Region IS NOT NULL to the existing predicate.
options.why: This explicitly excludes the required null-to-value transition rather than detecting it.

options.text: It misses the change; add t.Region IS NULL AND s.Region IS NULL as an OR branch.
options.why: That flags two nulls as changed and still does not match the one-null transition shown here.

options.text: It misses the change; include explicit one-null comparisons as well as unequal non-null values.
options.why: Null transitions must be recognized separately when using ordinary inequality.

explanation: A WHERE predicate keeps true rows, not unknown rows. Make null handling part of the change contract.
code:
WHERE t.Region <> s.Region
-- Target: NULL; Source: 'East'

title: Select a collision-free null comparison
prompt: NULL and an empty string are distinct allowed Region states. Which expression detects all changes without conflating those states?

options.text: t.Region <> s.Region OR (t.Region IS NULL AND s.Region IS NOT NULL) OR (t.Region IS NOT NULL AND s.Region IS NULL)
options.why: This detects unequal values and each one-null transition while treating two nulls as unchanged.

options.text: COALESCE(t.Region, '') <> COALESCE(s.Region, '')
options.why: Mapping NULL to an allowed empty string loses the distinction required here.

options.text: t.Region <> s.Region OR t.Region = NULL OR s.Region = NULL
options.why: Equality to NULL remains unknown and does not repair null transitions.

options.text: t.Region IS NULL OR s.Region IS NULL
options.why: This falsely flags two nulls and misses two different non-null values.

explanation: A substitution value is safe only if it cannot collide with a valid domain value. The question explicitly permits empty strings.

title: Skip an unchanged replay
prompt: A canonical incoming row has the same tracked and type 1 attributes as the current target row. Its change identity has already been applied. Which normal outcome is appropriate?

options.text: Insert another version to preserve the new processing timestamp, even though the source change identity is already applied.
options.why: Execution audit history can be separate; a repeated business change should not create another attribute version.

options.text: Update the existing version's ValidFrom to the retry time so the row remains current.
options.why: Moving the recorded start creates an artificial gap or changes the time assignment of existing facts.

options.text: Do not add a version; recognize the applied identity and retain the existing chain.
options.why: The state and change identity both establish that no additional business change is needed.

options.text: Rebuild this customer's versions from the current staged row, keeping only its latest value.
options.why: A current row cannot recreate the earlier captured chain, and the replay does not justify removing it.

explanation: SCD2 version growth should reflect intended tracked changes, not batch count. Replay protection is an explicit loader property.

title: Avoid reading changes after expiration
prompt: A loader finds changed customers by joining source to target WHERE target.IsCurrent = 1. It expires all those target rows, then reruns that same query to insert replacements. No current row remains for those customers. Which repair addresses the defect?

options.text: Keep the two queries but add a NOT ENFORCED foreign key.
options.why: Metadata does not restore the candidate rows removed by the current-row predicate.

options.text: Materialize the candidate replacements before expiration, then use that staged set for both writes in one transaction.
options.why: The stable candidate set survives the target-state change and keeps the write set coherent.

options.text: Insert replacements only when the post-expiration query returns zero rows.
options.why: A count alone does not retain the attributes, identities, and boundaries of each replacement.

options.text: Set every historical row current before rerunning the query.
options.why: This breaks the current-version invariant and creates conflicting candidates.

explanation: Atomicity is necessary, but it cannot correct a logically empty replacement query. Preserve the change set before mutating its source predicate.

title: Preserve a referenced surrogate
prompt: A dimension with generated surrogate keys is truncated and reloaded from today's source, generating different keys. Historical facts retain their old keys. What is the main modeling risk?

options.text: Only descriptions change; keys never matter after fact loading.
options.why: Fact references depend on the stored key values remaining meaningful.

options.text: The semantic model automatically remaps old keys from their numeric order.
options.why: Relationships match values, not an inferred ordering of generated identifiers.

options.text: SCD2 intervals can reconstruct all old versions from the current snapshot.
options.why: Current source values do not contain the discarded historical states.

options.text: Historical references can become orphaned or point to different members, and captured history can be lost.
options.why: Regeneration can invalidate fact linkage while the current-only source cannot recover history.

explanation: Preserve persistent version identities. A full rebuild requires an explicit coordinated migration and historical evidence, not a casual truncate/reload.

title: Choose a writable execution surface
prompt: The video demonstrates T-SQL updates to a Warehouse. A team tries the same UPDATE against a Lakehouse Delta table through its SQL analytics endpoint. Which route is appropriate?

options.text: Use a supported Lakehouse write engine such as Spark for the Delta table, or perform Warehouse DML on a Warehouse table.
options.why: Write through the engine that owns and supports the intended table changes.

options.text: Copy the Delta data to a Warehouse table, update the copy, and expect the original Lakehouse table to change without a write-back.
options.why: DML on a separate Warehouse copy changes that copy, not the original Delta table.

options.text: Create a SQL endpoint view showing the replacement attribute and treat that as a persisted update to the Delta table.
options.why: A query projection can change what consumers see, but does not persist the required table mutation.

options.text: Wrap the UPDATE in a transaction executed through the Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint.
options.why: Atomic grouping does not add a DML capability that the execution surface does not support.

explanation: Translate the pattern across engines deliberately. An SCD concept can be implemented with different supported write surfaces.

title: Trace two SCD3 changes
prompt: A row starts CurrentRegion = West and PreviousRegion = NULL. Each genuine change copies CurrentRegion to PreviousRegion, then writes the new CurrentRegion. Changes occur West -> East -> North. What remains?

options.text: Current = North; Previous = West.
options.why: The second change shifts East into Previous, replacing West.

options.text: Three rows with separate surrogate keys.
options.why: This specified type 3 operation updates columns on one existing row.

options.text: Current = North; Previous = East; West is no longer represented in these two columns.
options.why: The two-column pattern retains the latest value and exactly one previous value.

options.text: Current = East; Previous = North.
options.why: That reverses the final current and prior states.

explanation: Type 3's limited history cannot answer an arbitrary earlier as-of query after repeated changes.

title: Apply the type 3 roll-forward
prompt: A product has CurrentPrice = 60, PreviousPrice = 50. A validated change sets price to 70. Which conceptual assignment produces the intended limited history?

options.text: PreviousPrice = 50; CurrentPrice = 70
options.why: This keeps the initial prior value rather than the immediately previous price.

options.text: PreviousPrice = old CurrentPrice; CurrentPrice = 70
options.why: The saved old current value becomes the new previous value.

options.text: CurrentPrice = old PreviousPrice; PreviousPrice = 70
options.why: This reverses the roles and does not apply the new price as current.

options.text: Insert another row, leaving both rows marked current.
options.why: This changes the table grain and creates competing current rows rather than the stated column update.

explanation: Read 'old CurrentPrice' as the pre-update value. Store that value before replacing the current attribute in the implementation.

title: Reject limited history for an audit
prompt: A compliance report needs the territory effective on any sale date across five years and any number of territory moves. The source can supply reliable effective changes. Which dimension pattern meets the requirement?

options.text: SCD1 with one audit-last-modified timestamp.
options.why: One overwrite timestamp does not retain the prior territories and intervals.

options.text: SCD3 with CurrentTerritory and PreviousTerritory only.
options.why: Two attribute values cannot preserve an unbounded sequence of assignments.

options.text: SCD0 and the latest territory copied into the original row.
options.why: That violates the immutable policy and still lacks historical intervals.

options.text: SCD2 with persistent version keys and validated effective intervals used by fact loading.
options.why: Retained versions and unambiguous event-time mapping support the specified historical questions.

explanation: The history depth and as-of requirement determine the policy. A convenient previous-value column is insufficient here.

title: Keep transaction economics
prompt: A product's current list price changes from 50 to 70. A prior fact stores Quantity = 2 and TransactionUnitPrice = 45. The report needs actual revenue after discount. What should its measure use?

options.text: Sum Quantity * TransactionUnitPrice at line grain; the old line contributes 90.
options.why: The captured transaction price preserves the actual sale economics.

options.text: Multiply Quantity by today's list price; the old line contributes 140.
options.why: This restates the old sale at a later list price rather than its actual discounted price.

options.text: Multiply Quantity by the initial list price; the old line contributes 100.
options.why: The initial list price is also different from the captured transaction price.

options.text: Sum the dimension's current price once per product and ignore Quantity.
options.why: That does not calculate sales revenue at the stated line grain.

explanation: A price attribute and a transaction measure answer different questions. Dimension history alone does not preserve discounted sale amounts.

title: Model rapidly varying observations
prompt: A trading platform records each instrument price every second. Analysts require time-series statistics at instrument-second grain. Customer segmentation changes infrequently. Which design best fits these distinct rates and purposes?

options.text: Create a customer SCD2 version for every instrument price tick.
options.why: Instrument observations are unrelated to changes in the customer's segmentation attributes.

options.text: Keep only the latest instrument price in a type 1 dimension.
options.why: Overwriting discards the requested price time series.

options.text: Store instrument price observations in a fact at the required grain; track customer segmentation history separately when needed.
options.why: Observation history and descriptive customer changes are modeled independently.

options.text: Store two instrument prices in SCD3 and use them for all past seconds.
options.why: Two values cannot support the requested second-level time series.

explanation: Do not force a rapidly varying numeric observation into dimension-version growth when the required analysis is a time series of measurements.

title: Complete an inferred member
prompt: A late-arriving customer was inserted as inferred SK 900 and already referenced by facts. Its first descriptive details now arrive. No actual business change is known. What is the appropriate treatment?

options.text: Create SK 901 as a new historical version and leave SK 900 permanently unknown.
options.why: The new details complete the known entity; they do not establish a later business state.

options.text: Update the inferred row's details in place, clear its inferred flag, and preserve SK 900.
options.why: Completing that row lets already linked facts gain the intended descriptions.

options.text: Delete SK 900 and generate a replacement without remapping facts.
options.why: Existing facts would lose the referenced dimension member.

options.text: Ignore the details because SCD2 rows can never be corrected.
options.why: SCD2 does not prevent inferred-row completion or governed corrections.

explanation: Distinguish missing-details completion from a genuine effective attribute change. This question explicitly identifies an inferred member.

title: Map historical assignments
prompt: For Northwind, which CustomerSK sequence belongs to Sale A, Sale B, and Sale C when preparing historical sales?

options.why: This restates all events to today's East assignment rather than their event-time versions.
Sale B is exactly the new interval's inclusive start, not the old interval's end.
Sale C occurs after the East version begins and cannot map to expired West.
March 31 belongs to West; the boundary and May sale belong to East.

explanation: Resolve each event independently against the supplied half-open intervals. Arrival time does not change these event-time mappings.

title: Compare history and restatement
prompt: For Northwind, compare historical regional totals with the separate report that deliberately uses today's region for every sale. Which pair is correct?

options.text: Historical: West 100, East 500. Restated: East 600, West 0.
options.why: The historical map separates Sale A; deliberate current-state restatement assigns all three to East.

options.text: Historical: West 300, East 300. Restated: East 600, West 0.
options.why: The boundary sale belongs to East, so West does not include its amount 200.

options.text: Historical: West 100, East 500. Restated: West 100, East 500.
options.why: The separate current-state report intentionally uses today's East label for every event.

options.text: Historical: West 600, East 600. Restated: East 1200, West 0.
options.why: These totals imply repeated matches instead of one assignment for each sale.

explanation: Both report semantics are valid when explicit. Historical and restated groupings each reconcile to the same fact total of 600.

title: Keep both reporting meanings
prompt: Northwind needs historical assignment and today's-region restatement in one analytics solution. Select TWO appropriate design decisions.

options.text: Replace every fact's historical SK with 72 whenever the customer moves.
options.why: That discards the persisted event-time identity needed for historical reporting.

options.text: Retain each fact's resolved historical CustomerSK and the version dimension.
options.why: The existing version linkage preserves the event-time assignment.

options.text: Connect facts to all version rows using CustomerId and sum the result.
options.why: An unrestricted natural-key join multiplies events rather than selecting one current assignment.

options.text: Provide a separate current-customer projection with one row per CustomerId and a deliberate key path from historical versions to current assignments.
options.why: A unique current mapping can support restatement without overwriting historical fact keys.

explanation: Separate relationship paths or prepared reporting views can implement these meanings. Validate the chosen model's filter paths and current-key uniqueness; do not assume one repeated natural key is a one-side key.

title: Apply a cross-version correction
prompt: Northwind receives a corrected email and requires that correction to appear for all of C7's historical sales. Territory history must stay intact. What should change?

options.text: Insert a new territory version solely for the email correction.
options.why: It introduces unwanted history and does not fix email on the earlier referenced versions.

options.text: Update only SK 72 and delete SK 71.
options.why: This removes the West context required for Sale A.

options.text: Update Email on both C7 versions without changing their SKs, territories, or effective intervals.
options.why: The explicitly global correction applies to every version while preserving assignment history.

options.text: Overwrite both territories with East and preserve the old email.
options.why: This changes the protected history and fails to apply the actual correction.

explanation: The case supplies a global type 1 correction policy. Its scope must include all retained versions, rather than implicitly updating only the current row.

title: Derive actual revenue
prompt: For Fabrikam, what is total actual revenue after the July sale?

options.why: This uses historical list prices (2 * 50 + 3 * 70), not transaction prices.
This prices all five units at today's list price 70.
The first line is 2 * 45 = 90 and the second is 3 * 65 = 195.
Adding unit prices 45 + 65 ignores the quantities on both lines.

explanation: Sum line economics: 90 + 195 = 285. List prices answer a different question from actual discounted revenue.

title: Compare the two history structures
prompt: After Fabrikam applies the two genuine price changes, which stored-state comparison is correct?

options.text: SCD2 has three versions; the SCD3 summary is one row with CurrentPrice 70 and PreviousPrice 60.
options.why: Version history retains all three states while the two-column summary retains only the latest pair.

options.text: Both designs contain three rows with prices 50, 60, and 70.
options.why: The supplied SCD3 summary overwrites columns on its original row.

options.text: SCD2 has one row with 70; SCD3 has three surrogate-key versions.
options.why: This reverses the stated history mechanisms.

options.text: SCD2 has three versions; SCD3 CurrentPrice is 70 and PreviousPrice is 50.
options.why: The second roll-forward replaces PreviousPrice with the immediately preceding 60.

explanation: Count versions separately from columns. The summary's overwritten earlier value cannot support the same unrestricted history as SCD2.

title: Quantify a repeated-version join
prompt: Fabrikam accidentally joins each sale to every P8 version using only ProductId, then sums Quantity * TransactionUnitPrice. What total results?

options.why: That is the correct unmultiplied fact total, but each line matches three rows here.
Two copies per fact would yield this, but P8 has three stored versions.
This uses today's list price 70 and three copies, rather than the specified captured price expression.
The correct fact total 285 appears three times because of the unrestricted join.

explanation: The erroneous join multiplies both line amounts by three. A dimension's valid keys do not fix an incorrect join predicate.

title: Recover an unknown commit outcome
prompt: Alpine loses the acknowledgement after a possible commit. Select TWO actions that prevent a replay from creating an extra version.

options.text: Reconcile the stable source change identity against the transactionally recorded applied identities.
options.why: A committed business change can be recognized even if the execution acknowledgement was lost.

options.text: Generate a new effective timestamp and treat each retry as a new business change.
options.why: That invents a second interval for the same source change.

options.text: On an unapplied change, use the retained staged values and atomic expire/insert/control operation; on an applied change, do not reapply it.
options.why: The stable identity and atomic control write distinguish the two possible commit outcomes.

options.text: Assume an empty acknowledgement proves rollback and append a replacement row.
options.why: The case explicitly allows the acknowledgement to be lost after a successful commit.

explanation: Atomicity keeps the version writes and control record together; stable business identity makes reconciliation possible. Retry alone does not provide this behavior.

title: Prevent conflicting source candidates
prompt: Alpine receives two rows for one CustomerId with the same source change identity and different Region values. No authoritative precedence rule exists. What should happen before mutation?

options.text: Choose the lexicographically larger Region because it is deterministic.
options.why: Deterministic ordering does not establish which conflicting business value is correct.

options.text: Reject or quarantine the conflict and obtain an authoritative resolution before staging a canonical change.
options.why: The load contract requires one justified source row per customer, not an arbitrary winner.

options.text: Create two current versions with the same effective start.
options.why: The result violates the complete unambiguous chain and single-current-version requirements.

options.text: Take the row ingested last and record the duplicate as handled, despite having no source precedence rule.
options.why: Arrival order is not an authoritative resolution of two conflicting payloads with the same business change identity.

explanation: A source conflict is a data-quality decision. Do not disguise it as a key-generation or SQL ordering problem.

title: Verify invariants before release
prompt: Alpine has successfully run its write transaction. Select TWO checks that directly verify the required version-chain and fact-link integrity before release.

options.text: Confirm every table has a PK declaration and assume that guarantees uniqueness and orphan rejection.
options.why: The Fabric declarations are unenforced and cannot replace data checks.

options.text: Require exactly one physical row per CustomerId across the entire history.
options.why: SCD2 intentionally stores multiple historical versions per business identifier.

options.text: Validate unique surrogate keys, one current version per active customer, positive intervals, no overlaps, and no gaps within each customer's known covered period.
options.why: These checks verify the identity and complete interval-chain invariants supplied by the case.

options.text: Verify every published fact resolves to one existing version key consistent with its intended event-time assignment.
options.why: A unique intended mapping protects fact references and historical reporting semantics.

explanation: A transaction protects an atomic write set; it does not prove its business logic is valid. Validate the resulting chain and intended references.
